units.title: Hello, C
units.summary: Write your first C program, print text with `printf`, and learn how to compile and run it.

lesson.md: Every C program starts in a function called `main`. Here is a complete program that prints one line of text.

The first line, `#include <stdio.h>`, loads the **standard input and output** library. A file that ends in `.h` is called a **header**. It contains `printf`, the function that prints text. Without it, the compiler does not know `printf`.

`int main(void)` is where the program starts. `void` in the parentheses means that `main` takes no input. The curly braces `{` and `}` hold its statements, and every statement ends with a semicolon `;`. `return 0;` ends `main` and tells the system that the program finished without errors.

C is a **compiled** language: a program called a **compiler** translates your source code into a file that the computer can run. Save the code as `hello.c`. The command `cc hello.c -o hello` compiles it, and `-o hello` names the result `hello`. Then `./hello` runs the program.

The compiler checks your code before anything runs. If it finds a mistake, it prints an error with the file name and the line number, for example `hello.c:4:5: error`. Fix the first error first: the errors after it are often caused by it.
`printf` does not start a new line by itself. Inside a string, `\n` is the **newline** character. Without it, the next output continues on the same line.
The backslash `\` starts an **escape sequence**, a special character inside a string. `\n` is a new line, `\t` is a tab, `\"` is a double quote, and `\\` is a backslash.
C is case-sensitive: `Main` or `Printf` do not work. If you forget a `;`, the compiler stops with an error.

card: `int main(void) { ... }` is where the program starts

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store numbers and characters in variables of type `int`, `double` and `char`, and print them with `printf`.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a named place in memory that stores a value. In C, every variable has a **type**, and you write the type before the name. `int age = 30;` creates a variable `age` of type `int`, a whole number, with the value `30`.

`printf` can print values, too. Its first argument is the **format string**. Each **format specifier** in it, like `%d`, is a placeholder: `printf` replaces it with the next value after the comma. `%d` stands for an `int`.

`double` stores numbers with a decimal point, and `char` stores a single character in single quotes, like `'A'`. Each type has its own specifier: `%d` for `int`, `%f` for `double` and `%c` for `char`. You can put several specifiers in one format string. The values follow in the same order.
`%f` prints six digits after the decimal point. Write `%.2f` to get two digits; the value is rounded. Use `%%` to print the percent sign itself.

The `=` sign **assigns** a value: it stores the value on the right in the variable on the left. You can assign a new value later, but the type stays the same. You can also declare a variable first and give it a value later.
Write `const` before the type when a value must never change. The compiler then stops with an error if you try to assign a new value. In the next example, `*` means multiply.

A variable without a value contains garbage: whatever was in that memory before. Always give a variable a value before you read it. Also make sure the specifier matches the type: printing a `double` with `%d` gives wrong output.

card: `int n = 5;` whole number, `double x = 2.5;` decimal, `char c = 'A';` character

units.title: Operators
units.summary: Calculate with `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%`, understand integer division, and use `++`, `+=` and casts.

lesson.md: C has the usual arithmetic operators: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies and `/` divides. As in mathematics, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`. Use parentheses `(` `)` to change the order.

When both numbers are `int`, `/` is **integer division**: the result is a whole number, and the part after the decimal point is cut off. `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`. The **remainder operator** `%` gives what is left over: `7 % 2` is `1`.

If at least one number is a `double`, the division keeps the decimals, as `7.0 / 2` shows. The remainder `%` only works with whole numbers. It tells you if a number is even: `n % 2` is `0` for every even `n`.

Changing a variable based on its own value is very common, so C has short forms. `x += 5` means `x = x + 5`. There are also `-=`, `*=`, `/=` and `%=`. `x++` adds 1 to `x` (**increment**), and `x--` subtracts 1 (**decrement**).

Use `++` and `--` as statements of their own, like `count++;`. Inside bigger expressions they are hard to read, and some combinations, like `i++ + i++`, are not allowed in C and give unpredictable results.

Sometimes you have two `int` values but want a result with decimals. A **cast** converts a value to another type: write the type in parentheses before the value, like `(double)total`. Converting a `double` to an `int` cuts off the decimals.
`(double)(total / count)` is `3.0`, not `3.5`: the division inside the parentheses happens first, with whole numbers. Cast before you divide.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Make decisions with `if`, `else` and `switch`, compare values, and combine conditions with `&&`, `||` and `!`.

lesson.md: An `if` statement runs code only when a **condition** is true. The condition goes in parentheses, the code in curly braces. With `else`, you say what happens otherwise.

C compares with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. A comparison gives `1` when it is true and `0` when it is false. In a condition, `0` means false and every other number means true.
Do not confuse `=` and `==`. `if (x = 5)` does not compare: it assigns `5` to `x`, and the condition is always true. The compiler warns about it, so read the warnings.
Chain conditions with `else if`. C checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true.
`&&` means **and**: both sides must be true. `||` means **or**: at least one side must be true. `!` means **not**: it turns true into false and false into true.

`switch` compares one whole number or character with several fixed values. Each `case` is a value followed by a colon. `break` ends the `switch`. Without it, the program **falls through** and also runs the next case. `default` runs when no case matches.

card: `0` is false, every other number is true

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with `for`, `while` and `do`-`while`, and control loops with `break` and `continue`.

lesson.md: A **loop** repeats code. The `while` loop checks its condition before every round and runs the body as long as the condition is true.
If the condition never becomes false, the loop runs forever. Make sure the body changes something the condition depends on, like `n--` above.

A `for` loop puts everything for counting in one line, with three parts separated by `;`: the start (`int i = 1`), the condition (`i <= 3`) and the step (`i++`). The step runs after each round. The variable `i` exists only inside the loop.
The step can be any change, like `i += 2` or `i--`. A loop can also build a result: here `sum` starts at `0`, and every round adds the current number.
A `do`-`while` loop checks the condition **after** the body. So the body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false from the start. Note the `;` after the condition.
`break` leaves the loop immediately. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.

card: `break` leaves the loop, `continue` skips to the next round

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Split programs into functions with parameters and return values, declare them with prototypes, and understand scope.

lesson.md: A **function** is a named block of code that you can call again and again. You already know two: `main` and `printf`. A function definition starts with the **return type**, then the name and the **parameters** in parentheses.

`int square(int n)` says: the function is called `square`, it takes one `int` called `n`, and it gives back an `int`. `return` ends the function and hands the value back to the caller. The value you pass in the call, like `4`, is called an **argument**.
Separate several parameters with commas. If a function returns nothing, its return type is `void`. If it takes nothing, write `void` in the parentheses, as in `main(void)`.

C reads a file from top to bottom, so you must declare a function before you call it. If you want to define it below `main`, put a **prototype** above `main`: the first line of the function, ending with `;`.

Parameters and variables declared inside a function are **local**: they exist only inside that function, from their declaration to the closing `}`. The same is true for variables declared inside any block, such as a loop. So different functions can use the same names without conflict.
C passes arguments **by value**: the function gets a copy. If it changes its parameter, the variable of the caller stays the same.
To change a variable of the caller, a function needs the address of that variable. You will learn how in the unit about pointers.

card: `void` means no return value, `(void)` means no parameters
`int max(int a, int b);` is a prototype above `main`
Arguments are copied, local variables live only in their block

units.title: Arrays and strings
units.summary: Store many values in arrays, loop over them, and work with strings as `char` arrays using `string.h`.

lesson.md: An **array** stores several values of the same type, one after another. You write the size in square brackets `[ ]` and the values in curly braces. Each element has an **index**, starting at `0`: `scores[0]` is the first element.
An array with 4 elements has the indexes `0` to `3`. C does not check the index: `scores[4]` reads memory that does not belong to the array, and the program may crash or print garbage.

`sizeof` gives the size of something in bytes. `sizeof(scores)` is the size of the whole array and `sizeof(scores[0])` the size of one element, so dividing them gives the number of elements. The result has the type `size_t`, a whole number that is never negative. You print it with `%zu`.
If you list the values, you can leave out the size, as in `int scores[] = {90, 75, 82, 60};`. The compiler counts the values for you.

C has no separate string type. A **string** is an array of `char` that ends with the **null character** `'\0'`. A string literal like `"cat"` adds it automatically, so `char word[] = "cat";` uses 4 bytes. Print a string with `%s`.

The header `<string.h>` has functions for strings. `strlen(s)` counts the characters before the `'\0'`. `strcpy(dest, src)` copies the string `src` into the array `dest`. `strcmp(a, b)` compares two strings and gives `0` when they are equal.
You cannot copy strings with `=` or compare them with `==`. Use `strcpy` and `strcmp` instead. The target array must be big enough for all characters plus the `'\0'`.

card: `sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])` is the number of elements
`char s[] = "hi";` ends with `'\0'`, print it with `%s`

units.title: Pointers and structs
units.summary: Use addresses with `&` and `*`, change variables through pointer parameters, and group data in a `struct`.

lesson.md: Every variable lives at an **address** in memory. The operator `&` gives the address of a variable. A **pointer** is a variable that stores an address: `int *p` declares a pointer to an `int`.
The operator `*` in front of a pointer **dereferences** it: it gives the value at that address. Through the pointer, you can read the variable and also change it.
The symbol `*` has several jobs. In a declaration, `int *p` means that `p` is a pointer. In an expression, `*p` means the value that `p` points to. And `a * b` is still a multiplication.

Remember that C copies arguments. If a function gets a pointer, it can change the caller's variable through it. You pass the address with `&`. In `add_one`, `(*n)++` needs the parentheses: it increases the value that `n` points to.
A pointer must point to a valid variable before you use `*` on it. Use `NULL` for a pointer that points nowhere, and never dereference a `NULL` pointer: the program crashes.
A `struct` groups several values, called **members**, into one new type. The definition ends with `};`. You reach a member with a dot, as in `p.x`.
With a pointer to a struct, use the arrow `->` to reach a member: `ptr->x` means `(*ptr).x`. Functions often take a pointer to a struct, so they can change it without copying it.

card: `struct Point { int x; int y; };` then `p.x`

exercises.prompt: What does this program print?
exercises.explain: `triple` gets the address of `v` and changes the value at that address, so `v` becomes `15`.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print?
exercises.explain: `it.qty` is `2` and `it.price` is `1.5`, so the product is `3.0`, printed with two decimals.

exercises.prompt: `p` is a pointer to a `struct Point`. How do you read its member `x`?
exercises.explain: With a pointer to a struct, you use the arrow `->`. The dot works only on the struct itself.
`p` stores the address of `x`, so `*p` is `x` itself.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap so `p` stores the address of `n`.
exercises.explain: `&n` is the address of `n`. A pointer to `int` stores such an address.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap so `reset` sets `count` to `0`.
exercises.explain: The parameter is a pointer, so you pass the address `&count`. Then `reset` can change `count`.

exercises.prompt: Build a line that sets the member `age` of the struct that `ptr` points to to `30`.
exercises.explain: `ptr->age` reaches the member `age` through the pointer, and `=` assigns the new value.

exercises.prompt: The program starts with `#include <stdio.h>`. Put the other lines in order so it prints `120`.
